JUDGMENT 


By means of order/reference no. L-402/27/20I2-IR(BI) dated 30.08.20l2, the Central Government 
considered it desirable to refer the dispute for adjudication to the following effect:- 


"Whether the action of the management of Northern Railway, Muradabad in terminating the services 
of Shri Sheetala Prasad S/o Shri Ramanand w. e. f 22/2/986, is legal and justified? To what relief the 
workman is entitled?" 


In pursuance to the said reference I.D. Case No. 68/202 registered before this tribunal. 


Thereafter claimant filed his statement of claim before this tribunal on 24.09.202 in which it has been stated that 
Shri Sheetal Prasad/ workman was initially engaged as casual labour on l6.0i.975 and in the said capacity work till 
2.2.986 however, his services were retrenched/termination on 22.2.986. 


Further in claim statement the relief as claimed by workman is that his termination/retrenchment, order dated 
22.2.[986 may be set aside, he may be reinstated service with all constitutional benefit. 


The respondent has filed written statement and thereafter the rejoinder and documents/evidence have been exchanged 
between parties. 


[भाग [I—Ve 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 3, 2026/07 3, 947 7667 


On behalf of respondent a plea was taken that as per the case of workman, his services was retrenchment on 
22.2.986, for redressed of his grievances approached the authority in the year 202. 


Thereafter reference was made on 30.08.202, so the case filed by the workman is able to be dismissed on the ground 
of delay and he is not entitled for any relief. 


FINDING AND CONCLUSION 


As per to the admitted facts of the present case, the claimant/workman was engaged as casual labour on 24.09.202, 
and his services was retrenched/terminated on 22.2.986. 


Thereafter for redressal of his grievances approached the authority in the year 202, the present reference has been 
made on 30.08.202, filed his claim statement on 24.09.202, before this tribunal. 


In view of the said facts the claim statement filed by workman against his retrenchment/termination, dated 
22.2.986, was after l6 years, so the same is highly belated as such he is not entitled for any relief in view of the law 
which are quoted here in below: 


In Nedungadi Bank Ltd. vs. K.P. Madhavankutty and Ors. 2000 (2) SCC 455 it was noted at paragraph 6 as 
follows: 


"6. Law does not prescribe any time-limit for the appropriate Government to exercise its powers under 
Section 709 of the Act. It is not that this power can be exercised at any point of time and to revive matters 
which had since heel) settled. Power is to be exercised reasonably and in a rational manner. There appears 
to us to be no rational basis on which the Central Government has exercised powers in this case after a 
lapse of about seven years of the order dismissing the respondent from ser-vice. At the time reference was 
made no industrial dispute existed or could be even said to have been apprehended. A dispute which is stale 
could not be the subject-matter of reference under Section 79 of the Act. As to when a dispute can be said to 
be stale would depend on the facts and circumstances of each case. When the matter has become final, it 
appears to us to be rather incongruous that the reference be made under Section 79 of the Act in the 
circumstances like the present one. In fact it could be said that there was no dispute pending at the time 
when the reference in question was made. The only ground advanced by the respondent was that two other 
employees who were dismissed from service were reinstated. Under what circumstances they were dismissed 
and subsequently reinstated is nowhere mentioned. Demand raised by the respondent for raising an 
industrial dispute was ex-facie bad and incompetent." 


Further, in S.M. Nilajkar and Ors. v. Telecom District Manager, Karnataka 2003 (4) SCC 27 the position was 
reiterated as follows: (at para 7) 


#77, It was submitted on behalf of the respondent that on account of delay in raising the dispute by the 
appellants the High Court was justified in denying relief to the appellants. We cannot agree. It is true, as 
held in M/s. Shalimar Works Ltd. v. Their Workmen (supra) AIR 7959 SC 7277), that merely because the 
Industrial Disputes Act does not pro-vide for a limitation for raising the dispute it does not mean that the 
dispute can be raised at any time and without regard to the delay and reasons therefor. There is no 
limitation prescribed for reference of disputes to an industrial tribunal, even so it is only reasonable that the 
disputes should be referred as soon as possible after they have arisen and after conciliation proceedings 
have failed particularly so when disputes relate to discharge of workmen wholesale. A delay of 4 years in 
raising the dispute after even reemployment of the most of the old workmen was held to be fatal in M/ s. 
Shalimar Works Limited v. Their Workmen (supra) AIR 7959 SC 7277, In Nedungadi Bank Ltd. v. K.P. 
Madhavankutty and others (supra) AIR 2000 SC 839, a delay of 7 years was held to be fatal and disentitled 
to workmen to any relief. In Ratan Chandra Sammanta and others v Union of India and others (supra) /993 
AIR SCW 2244, it was held that a casual labourer retrenched by the employer deprives himself of remedy 
available in law by delay itself, lapse of time results in losing the remedy and the right as well. The delay 
would certainly be fatal if it has resulted in material evidence relevant to adjudication being lost and 
rendered not available. However, we do not think that the delay in the case at hand has been so culpable as 
to disentitle the appellants for any relief. Although the High Court has opined that there was a delay of 7 to 9 
years in raising the dispute before the Tribunal but we find the High Court factually not correct. The 
employment of the appellants was terminated sometime in /965-86 or /986-67., Pursuant to the judgment in 
Daily Rated Casual Employees Under P&T Department v. Union of India (supra) AIR 7/967 SC 2342, the 
department was formulating a scheme to accommodate casual labourers and the appellants were justified in 
awaiting the outcome thereof. On 76-7-/999 they were refused to be accommodated in the scheme. On 28- 
42-/990 they initiated the proceedings under the Industrial Disputes Act followed by conciliation 
proceedings and then the dispute was referred to the Industrial Tribunal cum-Labour Court. We do not think 
that the appellants deserve to be non suited on the ground of delay." 


7668 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 3, 2026/PAUSHA 3, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


The Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Krishi Utpadan Mandi Samity vs. Pahal Singh reported in 2007 2 SCC 
93 and more particularly paragraph Nos. l0, l, which read as under:- 


709, The Labour Court was also under an obligation to consider as to whether any relief, if at all could be 
granted in favour of the workman in view of the fact that the industrial dispute had been raised after ॥6 
years. It was obligatory on the part of the Labour Court to consider that the respondent was in employment 
for very short period. It had also not arrived at a finding that the respondent was in continuous service 
within the meaning of Section 2(g) of the U.P. Industrial Disputes Act or for that matter in terminating the 
ser-vices of the respondent, the appellant did not comply with the requirements of law particularly Section 6- 
N thereof. In absence of such a finding, the High Court in our opinion should have interfered with the 
Award. 


३. It is now well-settled principle of law that "delay de-feats equity". 
(see also Haryana State Co-operative Land Development Bank vs. Neelam (2005) 5 SCC 97 ) 


Further, in the present case, it is also not in dispute rather admitted by the workman has raised his grievance to be 
included in screening for year 983-84 by means of raising industrial dispute in the year 2003, which was referred to 
this Tribunal after 20 years, as such, he is not entitled for any relief. Because, Hon'ble Rajasthan High Court, Jaipur 
Bench, in the case of M.D./Chief Manager, Jaipur Agar, Rajasthan State Road Transport Corp., Jaipur vs. 
General Secretary, Rajasthan Transport Workers Organisation, Jaipur, 2024 (82) FLR 892, has held as under: 


"6. In the case at hand, the respondent-workman was appointed on the post of Driver vide order dated 
47.72./966. Accordingly, the benefit of first selection scale became due after nine years, sometime in 2004 - 
2005. The same was not done and neither was the non-grant of the benefit at the time was challenged by the 
respondent-workman. The benefit of first selection scale was only granted vide order dated 06.04.2004. This 
deferment was also not challenged immediately and was only challenged for the first time in 20/3, The first 
issue that is to be decided by this Court is what effect, if any, would this delay have on the merits of the case. 


7. To decide the first issue, recourse may be taken to Hon'ble Supreme Court judgment of Mohan Lal (supra), the 
relevant portion of which is reproduced as under: 


7॥9, We are clearly of the view that though the Limitation Act, 963 is not applicable to the reference made 
under the ID Act but delay in raising industrial dispute is definitely an important circumstance which the 
Labour Court must keep in view at the time of exercise of discretion irrespective of whether or not such 
objection has been raised by the other side. The legal position laid down by this Court in Gitam Singh [Asstt. 
Eng., Rajasthan Development Corpn. v. Gitam Singh], that before exercising its judicial discretion, the 
Labour Court has to keep in view all relevant factors including the mode and manner of appointment, nature 
of employment, length of service, of service, the ground on which termination has been set aside and the 
delay in raising industrial dispute before grant of relief in an industrial dispute, must be invariably followed. 


20. Now, if the facts of the present case are seen, the position that emerges is this: the workman worked as a 
work-charged employee for a period from 7./7./964 to 77.2./966 (in all he worked for 286 days during his 
employment). The services of the workman were terminated with effect from 46., 2, /986, The workman raised 
the industrial dispute in /992 i.e. after 6 years of termination. The Labour Court did not keep in view 
admitted delay of 6 years in raising the industrial dispute by the workman. The judicial discretion exercised 
by the Labour Court is, thus, flawed and unsustainable. The Division Bench of the High Court was clearly in 
error in restoring the award of the Labour Court whereby reinstatement was granted to the workman. 
Though, the compensation awarded by the Single Judge was too low and needed to be enhanced by the 
Division Bench but surely reinstatement of the workman in the facts and circumstances is not the 
appropriate relief." 


Further, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Sadhu Singh (supra), held as under: 


"6. We shall at the outset deal with the issue of limitation. The respondent was retired compulsorily from 
service on 4.47.2093. Original Civil Suit No. 47 of 2079 was instituted in 2070, The trial Judge as well as the 
first appellate court were of the view that the suit was not barred by limitation since the representation of the 
respondent for the grant of the three selection grades was rejected on 76.7/.2070, The first appellate court, 
while concurring with the trial Judge also noted that the "final request" made by the respondent-plaintiff on 
46.47.2040 was rejected and hence the suit was within limitation. 


7. The respondent waited for seven long years after his retirement to pursue a claim for the grant of selection 
grade. This was clearly beyond the residuary period of limitation of three years provided in Article 37 of 
the Schedule to the Limitation Act, /963, That apart, in the decision of this Court in State of Rajasthan v. 
Shankar Lal Parmar, the Court has considered the ambit of the scheme for selection grade. This Court has 
held thus: 


[भाग ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 3, 2026/पौष 3, 947 7669 


"6. Another important and relevant clause in the said order for our perusal is Clause 7, which is also 
reproduced hereinbelow: 


7. Selection grades in terms of this order shall be granted only to those employees whose record of service is 
satisfactory. The record of service which makes one eligible for promotion on the basis of seniority shall be 
considered to be satisfactory for the purpose of grant of the selection grade. 


7. Clause 7 makes it clear that only those employees would be entitled for grant of selection grades, whose 
service record has been satisfactory and are otherwise eligible for promotion on the basis of seniority but 
have not been able to get the same as there might not be any channel of promotion or for want of sanctioned 
posts in the cadre." 


&. The Court held that in terms of Clause 7, only those employees whose service record has been satisfactory 
could be entitled to be granted selection grade. In this context, the Court held: 


77, Clause 7 further makes it clear that only those/such employees would be entitled to be granted selection 
grade whose service record has been satisfactory. This implicitly shows that the person who has an 
untainted, unblemished, clean and unpolluted record in service would be treated on a higher pedestal than 
those who have either tainted, blemished, unclean or polluted record. This obviously appears to be a 
reasonable classification and is under the ambit and touchstone of Article 74 of the Constitution. There is 
neither any ambiguity nor any doubt in the same." 


9. On the touchstone of the above principles, it is evident that the respondent had been subjected to several 
disciplinary proceedings and as many as 79 charge- sheets were issued against him which resulted in 
penalties of a varying nature. The service record of the respondent cannot be regarded as untainted or clean. 


409. Ms Nidhi, learned counsel for the respondent submitted that some of the penalties which were imposed 
on the respondent were without cumulative effect. The consequence of the withholding of increments without 
cumulative effect is that after the period prescribed, the respondent would be entitled to restoration of the 
original pay scale or the original pay. However, this does not obviate the position that the imposition of the 
penalty itself indicates that the service record of the employee was not satisfactory. Another submission 
which has been urged is that the penalties were of a minor nature. Assuming that to be so, it is evident that 
for the grant of selection grade, the respondent did not fulfil the requirements of a clean record of service. 
The grant of the selection grade is not a matter of right and was subject to the terms and conditions which 
were stipulated. The respondent failed to fulfil these terms and conditions. 


I]. For the above reasons, we are of the view that both on the question of limitation as well as on merits, the 
respondent was not entitled to the relief which was sought. The suit instituted by the respondent resp seven 
years after he had demitted office was barred by limitation. That apart, the respondent failed to meet the 
basic requirements for the selection grade." (Emphasis supplied) 


Further, the Hon'ble Supreme Court, in Bichitrananda Behera (supra), after considering the erstwhile 
judgments of Union of India v. Tarsem Singh, Union of India v. N. Murugesan, and Chairman, State Bank of 
India v. M.J. James, concluded that delay and laches are vital in service matters, and can be seen as 
acquiescence." 


AWARD 


For the foregoing reasons the workman is not entitled for any relief as per the Reference No. L-40i2/27/202-IR(B- 
I) dated 30.08.202 and the same is answered accordingly.

0. Thereafter, respondents had gone in writ petition bearing CWP No.22648 of 2025 against the said order and 
Hon'ble High Court in its decision dated 3.08.2025 (Annexure G) has held that directions given by Hon'ble CAT 
Chandigarh on 2.03.2025 (Annexure F) to implement order dated |8.02.20I9 (Annexure E) be complied with and

Il. On the other hand, Id. counsel for the management contended that compensation was paid to the applicants 
along with other workers at the time of their retrenchment. The applicants were purely daily wagers and now the 
military farm stands closed. Hence, the applicants are not entitled for their continuation in the service and cannot be

2. I have given due consideration to the arguments advanced by AR for both the parties. 


3. Before entering into the actual controversy between the parties, it will be pertinent to mention those facts 
which are admitted between the parties. It has been admitted by both the parties that currently Bir Dhantauri Military 
Farm stands closed. Under these circumstances, we are to see if applicants are workmen and respondent is an industry 
and if so, whether workmen are entitled for reinstatement from the date when their juniors were kept in service and 
all consequential benefits or otherwise what relief can be given to them. 


4. Now first question is whether the applicants are workman. In this regard, it is pertinent to mention here that 
onus to prove that workman are in the employment of respondent is always on the workmen/claimants and it is for the 
workmen to adduce evidence to prove the factum of his employment with the respondent. There is hardly any dispute 
with the preposition of law as propounded by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in several cases. In the present case, it has 
clearly been admitted by the respondents that applicants were appointed w.e.f. 07.04.990 as farm hand (daily wager) 
and they were retrenched in the year !999 and all the workmen were appointed through employment exchange. As 
such, it clearly establishes the relationship of employee and employer between the applicants and respondents. In this 
regard, reference can be made to the decision in the case of Devinder Singh Versus Municipal Council, Sanaur, 
AIR 20// Supreme Court 2532, wherein the Hon'ble Apex Court while interpreting the provisions of Section 2(S) of 
Act which deals with the definition of “workman” has observed as follows:- 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment/contract of 
service, the quantum of wages/pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a 
person is a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not 
make any distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There 
is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person employed on 
regular basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on 
temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours 
is not a workman.” 


5. It is clear from the perusal of aforesaid observation that even if a person is engaged on temporary, part time 
daily wages or contract basis or for doing any other kind of work and is duly paid wages for the said work, in that 
eventuality such a person would be covered by the definition of “workman” as provided under Section 2(s) of the 
Act. Thus, it is held that workmen were engaged on temporary basis. However, they fall under the definition of 
workman as stated above under Section 2(s) of the Act. 


6. The question which arises for consideration is whether the establishment Military Farm is an industry. The 
Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore_ Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa /9780(36) FLR 266 
dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression "industry" as defined in Section 2(J) of the Act, and has laid 
down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test is where (a) 
systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee(the direct and substantial element 
is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human wants and 
wishes prima facie is an "Industry" in that enterprise. Coming into the case in hand, the work assigned to the 
workmen relates to do work of catering animals and other related work for production of milk with the cooperation of 
the workmen and respondent. Thus, all the necessary ingredients of the above judgment are satisfied. 


7. It is also mentioned here that workmen were not regular employees of the respondent as regular employees 
are governed by Central Civil Service Rules. The workmen, who were casual workers, are not governed by the 
aforesaid rules and are governed by the Act and if any dispute arises, the same is governed by the Act. 


8. Further, Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Chief Conservator of Forest Versus Jagannath Maruti 
Kondhare (7००6 (2) SCT 764), has held that work, which was not be regarded as a part of inalienable of inescapable

function of the State and which work can be well undertaken by a private agency does not require an instrumentality 
of State, such functions of the State fall within the ambit of Industry. Thus, function of doing diary cannot be said to 
be sovereign function of the State and thus for this purpose of industrial dispute, respondents would be termed as 
industry. 


9. Now next question, which arise for consideration is that whether workmen who were retrenched vide order 
dated 9.03.999 (Annexure B) and their juniors were also retrenched on the same date, they have not been offered 
employment in view of the Section 25H of the Act, which read as follows:- 


25H. Re-employment of retrenched workmen.—Where any workmen are retrenched, and the employer proposes 
to take into his employ any persons, he shall, in such manner as may be prescribed, give an opportunity 2 [to 
the retrenched workmen who are citizens of India to offer themselves for reemployment and such retrenched 
workman] who offer themselves for re-employment shall have preference over other persons.

Section 25T of the Act provides as under:- 


“25T. Prohibition of unfair labour practice.—No employer or workman or a trade union, whether registered under 
the Trade Unions Act, /926 (76 of /926), or not, shall commit any unfair labour practice.” 


26. It is also added here that applicants had filed OA No.l38-HR-92 seeking their regularization before the 
Hon'ble CAT, Chandigarh and vide order dated 28.07.!999 (Ex. ४४/५७४७।/6), the OA was dismissed. However, they 
remained in service due to status quo given vide order dated 23.09.992. However, due to dismissal of the OA vide 
order dated 28.07.999 (४5.0४५७|/6), they were removed from service on the same date on 28.07.999. Even CWP 
filed against the order dated 28.07.999 (Ex. ४४५७४|/6) was dismissed vide order dated 30.08.2006. However, main 
question involved in the said litigation was regarding the regularization. However, in the present case, applicants have 
sought relief of unfair labour practice under Section 25T and retaining of juniors under Section 25H of the Act. 


2s Thus, in view of the above, workmen were entitled for continuity in service as and when vacancy arises. 
However, this fact can also not be ignored that junior to the workmen were retained in service ignoring applicant. At 
this stage, Bir Dhanturi Military Farm does not exist. Hence, only remedy left with this Tribunal is to grant them 
compensation.

As per letter dated /0/20I9 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference 
has been made to this Tribunal under Section-l0 of Industrial Disputes Act, 947 (in short the ‘Act’) as per 
Notification No. L-420/67/208 (IR(DU)) dt. /0/209. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“Whether the action on the part of the management of SECL, Central Workshop, Korba (Chhattisgarh) in 
inflicting harsh punishment upon Sh. Raja Ram Kashtriya, Ex-clerk Grade-II by removing from service instead of 
giving lesser punishment on absenteeism ground is appropriate and justified? If not, what relief, Sh. Raja Ram 
Kashtriya espoused by the Secretary, Bhartiya Vikas theka mazdoor union are entitled to?” 


After registering the case on the basis of reference, notices were issued to the parties. They appeared and 
filed their respective statement of claim in defense. 


The case of the workman is mainly that while he was working as Clerk Grade-II with the management and 
was posted in Laxman Project, he was issued a charge sheet with respect to his unauthorized absence in the year 997 
and was terminated from the services. He was reinstated by management allowing his appeal and was transferred to 
Central Workshop. He was issued another charge sheet on 3.07.999, with an allegation of unauthorized and wilful 
absence from work w.e.f., 02.06.999 till date of charge sheet. Infact, he could not report at work place for this period 
of '’” months due to illness of his father. He could not inform the management about his absence due to urgency, he 
filed a reply to the charge sheet admitting the charges and assured that he will not repeat it. The management 
terminated his service vide order dated 06.02.200, he came to know about this order only on 22.05.2004 when he got 
the notice of management to vacate the accommodation allotted to him by management as he was terminated from 
service. He raised the dispute. After failure of conciliation, dispute was referred to this Tribunal. 


According to the workman, infact, he had not admitted the charges rather he had explained his absence, 
which was wrongly taken by management as his admission to the charges. The management thus, acted arbitrarily 
treating his explanation as his admission of guilt and the punishment is also hash. 


The case of the management is mainly that the services of the workman were dismissed vide order dated 
06.02.200I. The present dispute has been raised in the year 209, there is an unexplained delay of l8 years since, the 
records are old, they are no traceable with the management, the workman was habitual absentee. He was awarded 
previous punishments also for his unauthorized absence. He was once dismissed for his unauthorized absence but was 
reinstated allowing his mercy petition but he did not improve and absented himself unauthorizedly, an enquiry was 
conducted with respect to the charges of misconduct by way of absenting himself unauthorizedly from 02.06.999 to 
3.07.999. After management received no satisfactory reply to the charge sheet in the enquiry, the workman 
participated, the enquiry officer submitted the enquiry report holding the charges proved. The workman was issued a 
show cause notice on the enquiry report and thereafter the termination order dated 06.02.200I was passed. 


The enquiry papers were never produced before this Tribunal. According to management, they have weeded 
out as per Rules. Before this Tribunal, the workman has filed his affidavit as his Examination-in-chief, he has been 
cross-examined by management. The management did not examined any witnesses before this Tribunal also in proof 
of the charges. 


I have heard argument of Learned Counsel for workman Mr. Pranay Choubey and Mr. Neeraj Kewat, 
Learned Counsel for Management. I have gone through the record as well. 


The facts which emerge from the evidence on record, that according to the management, an enquiry was 
conducted with respect to charges, the enquiry papers or any document with respect to enquiry have not been 
produced by management. 


Case of the workman is that, no intimation was sent to him with respect to enquiry. The management had 
an opportunity to prove the charges before this Tribunal. 


In his affidavit, the workman has stated that he communicated his apologies to management to the charges 
which were wrongly treated as admission and he was terminated on the said basis, he admits that earlier also he was 
terminated for the same misconduct but was reinstated as an act of mercy. 


The absence of workman is not denied by him. It is also not his case that he had informed the management 
about his absence or had applied for leave or had taken any permission from management in this respect. The absence 
is of about two months, the workman was required to at least inform the management about his absence stating the 
ground of his absence. Since, he did not inform the management, with respect to his absence and did not seek any 
regularization of his absence, his conduct is no doubt a misconduct by way of unauthorized absence. 


As regards the punishment, this is also not disputed that the workman has been punished earlier also for the 
same charges. Hence, since he is a habitual offender, the punishment of his removal cannot be held to be 
disproportionate to the charges. 


7690 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 3, 2026/PAUSHA 3, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 
This is also established that the workman has raised dispute against termination of his services after l8 years, 
there is no explanation for this delay. In these circumstances, the workman is held entitled to no relief. 
On the basis of above discussion and findings, the reference deserves to be answered as follows:- 
AWARD 


Holding the action of the management of SECL, Central Workshop, Korba (Chhattisgarh) for dismissing 
Sh. Raja Ram Kashtriya, Ex-clerk Grade-II from services instead of giving lesser punishment on absenteeism 
ground, following Principles of Natural Justice is held to be legal and justified, he is entitled to no relief. 


No order as to cost.

As per letter dated 03/02/2020 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference is 
made to this Tribunal under Section-!0 of Industrial Disputes Act, 947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per Notification No. J- 
(I-3)/2020-IR dt. 03/02/2020. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“Whether the action of the management of M/s.PrimeOne Workforce Pvt. Ltd. and M/s. Kaapro 
Management Solutions Pvt. Ltd. in terminating the services of workman Shri Balram Chouhan working 
in the establishment of Registrar, Indian Institute of Technology, Indore (M.P.) wef. 76.02.2076 and 
28.04.20I6 respectively, are just & proper? If yes, what relief the workman concerned is entitled to and 
from which date?” 


Thereafter, corrigendum dated 22.07.2022 was received containing amended reference which is as follows: 


"Whether the action of the management of the Registrar, Indian Institute of Technology(IIT), Indore 
(M.P.) / M/s.PrimeOne Pvt. Ltd. and M/s. Kaapro Management Solutions Pvt. Ltd. in terminating the services of 
workman Shri Balram Chouhan working in the establishment of Registrar, Indian Institute of Technology, Indore 
(M.P.) w.ef. 76.02.2078 and 28.04.20I6 respectively, are just and Proper? If yes, what relief the workman 
concerned is entitled to and from which date? 


Notices were issued to both the parties. They appeared and filed their respective statement of claim and 
defense. 


The workman appeared and filed his statement of claim with copy of his appointment order, pay slip, 
dismissal order. 


IIT also appeared through their counsel. But did not file any written statement of defense. 


The Outsourcing Agency M/s Kaapro Industries and M/s Prime One Workforce did not appear inspite of 
service of notice, hence reference proceeded ex-parte against them. 


In evidence, the workman filed his affidavit as his examination-in-chief. None appeared for cross- 
examination. He also filed photocopy of his appointment letter, pay slip and dismissal order. 


I have heard argument of Learned Counsel for workman Mr. Pranay Choubey. None appeared for 
Management. I have gone through the record as well. 


The amended reference is the issued for determination in the case in hand. 


Case of the Workman is mainly that, IIT has issued an advertisement for Drivers, cleaners etc. by way of 
walk in interview. He appeared and was selected for cleaner. It was nowhere provided in the advertisement that he 
will be appointed through a private contractor. There was no role of a private contractor or outsourcing agency in his 
recruitment process as it was done by the IIT themselves. He was shown as outsourced employee of contractors 
supplied by them to IIT which is incorrect in fact, and is a camouflage adopted by Management of IIT just to deprive 
him of his admissible rights and benefits under the law. . 


He was disengaged by the outsourcing company M/s Prime One Workforce on !5.02.20l8 without any 
notice or compensation which is against law. He has sought his reinstatement with back wages and benefits as an 
employee of IIT. 

In evidence, he has filed his affidavit as his examination in chief and also has filed photocopy of letter 


extending his work contract, experience certificates, and dismissal order. 


Though, he has corroborated his allegations in his statement of claim, but the documents filed by him speak 
against his case. Letter of extension of his service contract dated 0.2.204 is issued by the Outsourcing agency 
M/s Kaapro Management. It shows that his service contract was extended further from .2.204 to 0.09.20I5 on 


7692 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 3, 2026/PAUSHA 3, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


previous conditions. Letter dated 27.04.207 is an another extension letter issued by M/s Prime One Workforce 
extending his work contract from 6.04.20I7 to 5.04.20I8 and letter dated 28.04.206 is the letter issued by 
Outsourcing Agencies M/s Kaapro Management Solutions disengaging him on expiry of his service contract. Letter 
dated 5.02.208 issued by M/s Prime One Workforce Outsourcing Agency has discontinued all his engagement by 
none extension of service contract. 


Hence, except his serving statement, there is nothing on record to show that the Workman was further 
employed by IIT and the Outsourcing Agency was a camouflage. It also comes out that, he was appointed by different 
agencies on contract basis and was discontinued on expiry of contract which is not a retrenchment as defined under 
Section 2(00) of the Act which is being reproduced as follows:- 


2 (00) "retrenchment" means the termination by the employer of the service of a workman for any reason 
whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action but does not include - 


(a) voluntary retirement of the workman; or 


(b) retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment 
between the employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulation in that behalf; or 


(bb) termination of the service of the workman as a result of the non-renewal of the contract of 
employment between the employer and the workman concerned on its expiry or of such contract 
being terminated under a stipulation in that behalf contained therein; or 


(c) termination of the service of a workman on the ground of continued ill-health; 


Also from evidence on record there is no employee employer relationship between him and the IIT is 
proved. 


In the light of above findings, the reference deserves to be answered against the Workman and is 
answered accordingly. 


No order as to cost.

As per letter dated 0/0/2020 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference is 
made to this Tribunal under Section-l0 of Industrial Disputes Act, l947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per Notification 
No. J-(4-2)/2020-IR dt. 0/0/2020. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“Whether the action of the management of M/s.PrimeOne Workforce Pvt. Ltd. and M/s.Kaapro 
Management Solutions Pvt. Ltd. in terminating the services of workman Shri Mukund Sharma working in 
the establishment of Registrar, Indian Institute of Technology, Indore (M.P.) w.e.f. 76.02.2078 and 
47.02.2076 respectively, are just & proper? If yes, what relief the workman concerned is entitled to and 
from which date?” 


Thereafter, corrigendum dated 22.07.2022 was received containing amended reference which is as follows: 


"Whether the action of the management of the Registrar. Indian Institute of Technology(IIT), Indore 
(M.P.)/ M/s.PrimeOne Pvt. Ltd. and M/s. Kaapro Management Solutions Pvt. Ltd. in terminating the services of 


7696 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 3, 2026/PAUSHA 3, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


workman Shri Mukund Sharma working in the establishment of Registrar. Indian Institute of Technology, Indore 
(M.P.) w.e.f. 76.02.2078 and 77.02.2076 respectively, are just and proper? If yes, what relief the workman 
concerned is entitled to and from which date?" 


Notices were issued to both the parties. They appeared and filed their respective statement of claim and 
defense. 


The workman appeared and filed his statement of claim with copy of his appointment order, pay slip, 
dismissal order. 


IIT also appeared through their counsel. But did not file any written statement of defense. 


The Outsourcing Agency M/s Kaapro Industries and M/s Prime One Workforce did not appear inspite 
of service of notice; hence reference proceeded ex-parte against them. 


In evidence, the workman filed his affidavit as his examination-in-chief. None appeared for cross- 
examination. He also filed photocopy of his appointment letter, pay slip and dismissal order. 


I have heard argument of Learned Counsel for workman Mr. Pranay Choubey. None appeared for 
Management. I have gone through the record as well. 


The amended reference is the issue for determination in the case in hand. 


Case of the Workman as taken by him in his statement of claim is mainly that, he was appointed by IIT as a 
Driver on !9.05.20 at consolidated salary and continued to work as a Driver till date of dismissal of his services 
which is 5.02.208. It is then, he came to known that his services have been shown through outsourcing agencies 
M/s Prime One Workforce which is incorrect on facts. In fact, he was appointed by IIT and continued to work for IIT 
as their employee. The Contractor or Outsourcing agency was simply a camouflage to deprive him the admissible 
benefits under law. He has further alleged that, his termination is bad in law and has requested his reinstatement as an 
employee of IIT with back wages and benefits. 


In his affidavit he has corroborated his allegations. 


His appointment letter dated !9.05.20, photocopy on record, filed by him, shows that it was for this month 
only and at consolidated pay of Rs. 0,000/- per month and for six months. Thus it was a fixed term appointment. 
There is nothing on record to show that this service contract was extended by IIT. The case of the Workman is further 
that, he was shown to be an outsourced employee, which is a camouflage as required to be proved by him, in which 
he has failed. 


The established facts that emerge are that, after his contract with IIT came to end, he would have been 
engaged through Outsourcing Agencies. Hence, there is no employee-employer relationship between him and IIT at 
the time he was disengaged by the Outsourcing Agency M/s Prime One. Hence, IIT cannot be fastened with any 
liability to reinstate or to compensate him. 


Since, his statement that he has worked for 240 days in a year and since 206, in which he has been shown 
as outsourced employee has been uncontroverted, hence he is held to have been proved his continuous engagement 
with the outsourcing agency M/s Prime One for more than 240 days at least in the year preceding his disengagement 
since his case that no notice or compensation was paid to him on his termination, his termination is held in violation 
of Section 25 F and 25G of the Act. 


As regards to the relief, keeping in view his tenure of engagement with the outsourcing agency M/s 
Prime One, he is held entitled to a lump sum compensation of Rs. 25,000/- in lieu of all his claims payable to 
him within 30 days from the date of publication of Award, failing which interest @6% per annum till payment. 


Reference stands answered accordingly.

As per letter dated 0/09/202 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference is 
made to this Tribunal under इस्टलांगा-0 of I.D. Act, 947 (in short the ‘Act’) as per reference number 
L-40/7/202/IR(DU) dt. 0/09/202. The dispute under reference related to :- 


“Whether the demand raised by Fire Brigade Karmachari Sangh, Jabalpur (M.P.) against the 
management of Ordnance Factory, Khamaria, Jabalpur to give 40 hours duty instead of 48 hours in a 
week and to give 5 days duty instead of 06 days to fire brigade section employees as per Ordnance Factory 
Board Letter No. 525/D/A/A(Pt)/V dated 73.05.7986, is proper, legal and justified ? If yes, to what relief 
the fire brigade section employees are entitled to ? What other directions, if any, are necessary in 
the matter ?” 


After registering the case on the basis of the reference received, notices were sent to the parties and were 
duly served on them. They appeared and filed their respective statements of claim and defense. 


In short, the case of the workman union is that the members of the union who are Fire Brigade Employees 
work with the management in their factory, the Defense Ordnance Factory Board issued a Circular No. 
525/D/A/A(pt)/V dated 3.05.988 for fixation of duty hours for grant of overtime allowances to four categories of its 
employees namely viz; Durbans, Fire Brigade Staff, Telephone Operators and Security Assistant, which provided that 
the these workmen shall qualify for overtime allowances for the work done above 44.I5 hours which was earlier 48 
hours a week. Case of the workman union is further that the management is not deputing them on work for a period 
more than 44.I5 hours in a week just to deny them the benefits of overtime allowances, which is unjust, illegal and 
arbitrary. 


Workman union has further prayed that the management be directed to depute the Fireman for 44 hours or 
more in a week of 6 days instead of 40 hours a week which is at present. 


[भाग II—ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 3, 2026/पौष 3, 947 7699 


Management did not appear and did not file any written statement of defense. 
The workman union filed affidavit of its Secretary and also the photocopy of the Circular mentioned above. 


I have heard argument of learned Counsel Mr. Arun Patel for the workman union. Management never 
participated in this case. I have gone through the record as well. 


The only issue of determination is whether the management can be obligated in law to depute the fireman 
on duty for more than 44.5 hours or 48 hours and more in a week, so that they may be entitled to overtime 
allowances. 


Settled principle is that working hours of a workman is fixed. If management employs the workman for 
working hours more than fixed as maximum, it is required to pay overtime for the additional hours, the workman has 
been on duty. If management takes work from its employee for a period less than what is fixed, there is no law to 
compel the management to take work from the workman for a period more than the workman is required to work, just 
to enable to workman to claim overtime that too when there is no provision that the employer is bound to employ the 
workman for a minimum period of hours on work. 


In the light of above discussion, the claim of the workman union fails and the reference is answered as 

follows :- 
AWARD 

Holding the demand raised by Fire Brigade Karmachari Sangh, Jabalpur (M.P.) against the 
management of Ordnance Factory, Khamaria, Jabalpur to give 40 hours duty instead of 48 hours in a week 
and to give 5 days duty instead of 06 days to fire brigade section employees as per Ordnance Factory Board 
Letter No. 525/D/A/A/A(Pt)//V dated 3.05.988, improper, illegal and unjustified, the fire brigade section 
employees are entitled to no relief. 


No order as to cost.

As per letter dated 28/0/209 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference is 
made to this Tribunal under Section-l0 of Industrial Disputes Act, l947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per Notification 
No. L-4202/203/208-(IR(DU)) dt. 28/0/209. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“Whether the Geological Survey of India is an Industry under the ID Act 7947, if so, whether the action 
of the Management of Geological Survey of India in terminating the services of Shri Mahesh 
Viswakarma, Drilling Helper #.०९.-३०/०४/2078 who was working on daily rated basis w.e.f. 04/02/7968 and 
completed more than 240 days in every Calendar year is fair and legal? If not, to what relief the workman 
is entitled to?” 


Notices were issued to both the parties. They appeared and filed their respective statement of claim and 
defense. 


Case of the Workman is mainly that, he was initially appointed as Drilling Helper by the Management vide 
its order dated 04.02.988 on daily rate basis, was posted under Unit In-charge Drilling Camp, Lalpur Distt. Shahdol 
and worked till 30.04.208 continuously for more than 240 days in every year. The Establishment is an ‘industry’ and 
an ‘industrial establishment’ is defined under the Act. The applicant is a ‘Workman’ as defined under the Act. The 
Act of termination of the Workman by Management is ‘retrenchment’ under the Act. According to the Workman, his 
termination by Management in spite of his continuous working from 04.02.988 to 30.04.20i8 without any notice or 
compensation is in violation of Section 25F and 25G of the Act. Also, it has been alleged that, the same category of 
the Workman engaged by Management after engagement of the Applicant Workman have been retained in service, 
hence the Management has acted in violation of Section 76 and 77 of the Industrial Disputes (Central) Rules, !956 (in 
short the ‘Rules’) in prohibiting the principle first come last go. Further, it has been alleged that the Management has 
adopted unfair practice by engaging the Workman as contract worker for 30 years which is prohibited under the Act. 
The Workman has thus prayed that holding the action of Management against law, the Workman be held entitled to 
be reinstated with back wages and consequential benefits. 


In its written statement of defense filed by the Management, they have pleaded that they are not an 
‘Industry’ as defined under Section 2(j) of the Act. The applicant is not a workman under the Act hence the reference

“The legal position may be summarized thus: The maxim contem-poranea exposito as laid down by Coke

the expressed intention of the legislature. It is perhaps difficult to attribute to a legislative body functioning in a 
Static society that its intention was couched in terms of considerable breadth so as to take within its sweep the 
future developments comprehended by the phraseology used. It is more reasonable to confine its intention only to 
the circumstances obtaining at the time the law was made. But in a modern progressive society it would be 
unreasonable to confine the intention of a legislature to the meaning attributable to the word used at the time the 
law was made, for a modern legislature making laws to govern a society which is fast moving must be presumed

services rendered, it could become an “industry”. When services are rendered by groups of charitable individuals to

462, This leads one on to consider another kind of test. It is that, wherever an industrial dispute could arise 
between either employers and their workmen or between workmen and workmen, it should be considered an area 
within the sphere of “industry” but not otherwise. In other words, the nature of the activity will be determined by the 
conditions which give rise to the likelihood of occurrence of such disputes and their actual occurrence in the sphere. 
This may be a pragmatic test. For example, a lawyer or a solicitor could not raise a dispute with his litigants in 
general on the footing that they were his employers. Nor could doctors raise disputes with their patients on such a 
footing. Again, the personal character of the relationship between a doctor and his assistant and a lawyer and his 
clerk may be of such a kind that it requires complete confidence and harmony in the productive activity in which they

systematised form of a business or trade, employing a number of persons, in which disputes could arise between 
employers and their employees, they would not enter the field of industry. The same type of activity may have both

juncture, it would be appropriate to recall the broader critique of indefinite “temporary” employment practices as done 
by a recent judgment of this court in Jaggo v. Union of India in the following paragraphs: - 


“22. The pervasive misuse of temporary employment contracts, as exemplified in this case, reflects a broader 
systemic issue that adversely affects workers’ rights and job security. In the private sector, the rise of the gig economy 
has led to an increase in precarious employment arrangements, often Civil Appeal No. 8558 of 208 characterized by 
lack of benefits, job security, and fair treatment. Such practices have been criticized for exploiting workers and 
undermining labour standards. Government institutions, entrusted with upholding the 


principles of fairness and justice, bear an even greater responsibility to avoid such exploitative employment practices. 
When public sector entities engage in misuse of temporary contracts, it not only mirrors the detrimental trends 
observed in the gig economy but also sets a concerning precedent that can erode public trust in governmental 
operations. 


25. It is a disconcerting reality that temporary employees, particularly in government institutions, often face 
multifaceted forms of exploitation. While the foundational purpose of temporary contracts may have been to address 
short-term or seasonal needs, they have increasingly become a mechanism to evade long-term obligations owed to 
employees. These practices manifest in several ways:- 


Misuse of “Temporary” Labels: - Employees engaged for work that is essential, recurring, and integral to the 
functioning of an institution are often labelled as “temporary” or “contractual,” even when their roles mirror those of 
regular employees. Such misclassification deprives workers of the dignity, security, and benefits that regular 
employees are entitled to, despite performing identical tasks. 


eArbitrary Termination: - Temporary employees are frequently dismissed without cause or notice, as seen in the 
present case. This practice undermines the principles of natural justice and subjects workers to a state of constant 
insecurity, regardless of the quality or duration of their service. 


¢ Lack of Career Progression: Temporary employees often find themselves excluded from opportunities for skill 
development, promotions, or incremental pay raises. They remain stagnant in their roles, creating a systemic disparity 
between Civil Appeal No. 8558 of 208 them and their regular counterparts, despite their contributions being equally 
significant. 

¢ Using Outsourcing as a Shield: - Institutions increasingly resort to outsourcing roles performed by temporary 
employees, effectively replacing one set of exploited workers with another. This practice not only perpetuates 
exploitation but also demonstrates a deliberate effort 


to bypass the obligation to offer regular employment. 


¢ Denial of Basic Rights and Benefits: - Temporary employees are often denied fundamental benefits such as 
pension, provident fund, health insurance, and paid leave, even when their tenure spans decades. This lack of social 
security subjects them and their families to undue hardship, especially in cases of illness, retirement, or unforeseen 
circumstances.” 


As we have observed in both Jaggo (Supra) and Shripal (Supra), outsourcing cannot become a convenient 
shield to perpetuate precariousness and to sidestep fair engagement practices where the work is inherently perennial. 
The Commission’s further contention that the appellants are not “full-time” employees but continue only by virtue of 
interim orders also does not advance their case. That interim protection was granted precisely because of the long 
history of engagement and the pendency of the challenge to the State’s refusals. It neither creates rights that did not 
exist nor erases entitlements that may arise upon a proper adjudication of the legality of those refusals. 


Before concluding, we think it necessary to recall that the State (here referring to both the Union and the 
State governments) is not a mere market participant but a constitutional employer. It cannot balance budgets on the 
backs of those who perform the most basic and recurring public functions. Where work recurs day after day and year 
after year, the establishment must reflect that reality in its sanctioned strength and engagement practices. The long- 


7708 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 3, 2026/PAUSHA 3, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


term extraction of regular labour under temporary labels corrodes confidence in public administration and offends the 
promise of equal protection. Financial stringency certainly has a place in public policy, but it is not a talisman that 
overrides fairness, reason and the duty to organise work on lawful lines. 


8. Moreover, it must necessarily be noted that “ad-hocism” thrives where administration is opaque. The 
State Departments must keep and produce accurate establishment registers, muster rolls and outsourcing 
arrangements, and they must explain, with evidence, why they prefer precarious engagement over sanctioned posts 
where the work is perennial. If “constraint” is invoked, the record should show what alternatives were considered, 
why similarly placed workers were treated differently, and how the chosen course aligns with Articles [4, 6 and 2] 
of the Constitution of India. Sensitivity to the human consequences of prolonged insecurity is not sentimentality. It is 
a constitutional discipline that should inform every decision affecting 


those who keep public offices running. 


9. Having regard to the long, undisputed service of the appellants, the admitted perennial nature of their duties, and 
the material indicating vacancies and comparator regularisations, we issue the following 


directions: - 


i. Regularization and creation of Supernumerary posts: All appellants shall stand regularized with effect from the 
date on which the High Court directed a fresh recommendation by the Commission and a fresh decision by the State 
on sanctioning posts for the appellants. For this purpose, the State and the successor establishment (U.P. Education 
Services Selection Commission) shall create supernumerary 


posts in the corresponding cadres, Class-III (Driver or equivalent) and Class-IV (Peon/Attendant/Guard or equivalent) 
without any caveats or preconditions. On regularization, each appellant shall be placed at not 


less than the minimum of the regular pay-scale for the post, with protection of last-drawn wages if higher and the 
appellants shall be entitled to the subsequent increments in the pay scale as per the pay grade. For seniority and 
promotion, service shall count from the date of regularization as given above. 


ii. Financial consequences and arrears: - Each appellant 


shall be paid as arrears the full difference between (a) the pay and admissible allowances at the minimum of the 
regular pay-level for the post from time to time, and 


(b) the amounts actually paid, for the period from 24.04.2002 until the date of regularization /retirement/death, as the 
case may be. Amounts 


already paid under previous interim directions shall be so adjusted. The net arrears shall be released within three 
months and if in default, the unpaid amount shall carry compound interest at 6% per annum from 


the date of default until payment. 


iii. Retired appellants: - Any appellant who has already retired shall be granted regularization with effect from 
24.04.2002 until the date of superannuation for pay fixation, arrears under clause (ii), and recalculation of pension, 
gratuity and other terminal dues. The revised 


pension and terminal dues shall be paid within three months of this Judgement. 


iv. Deceased appellants: - In the case of Appellant No. 5 and any other appellant who has died during pendency, 
his/her legal representatives on record shall be paid the arrears under clause (ii) up to the date of death, together with 
all terminal/retiral dues recalculated consistently with clause (i), within three months of this Judgement. 


These propositions of law and observations fully apply in the case in hand. 
In the light of above discussion and findings, the reference is answered as follows.

After registering the case on the basis of reference, notices were issued to the parties. They appeared and 
filed their respective statement of claim in defense. 


According to the workman union the claimant Devendra Goud was appointed against the vacant post of 
Peon by the then Branch Manager, Naiabadi Branch, Mandasaur on 9..2005 and worked 8 hours a day regularly 
till 02.06.203, when he was disengaged by the Bank without any notice or compensation. He had worked 
continuously for 240 days in every year and had discharged the duties of Peon for which he was paid his wages. He 
was paid bonus @ 8.33% whereas he was entitled to bonus @ 20% which is being paid by the other Banks. 
According to the union, this action of management is unjust, illegal and arbitrary. 


The union has requested that holding the action of management is unjust, illegal and arbitrary. He be held 
entitled to bonus @ 20% 


According to the management Bank, the claimant was engaged on daily wages purely on temporary basis 
in the branch on, as and when required basis. He worked purely on temporary basis intermittently when there was 
requirement, he worked 40 days in the year 2005-06, 20 days in 2007-08, 35 days in 2008-09, 79 days in 2009-0, 
44 days in 200-Il, 32 days in 20Ii-2 and 2 days in 203-4, for which he was paid his wages and bonus. The 
management Bank has denied the claim of the workman union that the workman worked continuously for a period of 
240 days and more in every calendar year.

chief, he has been cross-examined by management Bank. 


He filed and proved 7#-५७/।, Application before Labour Commissioner with respect to payment of bonus, 
Ex-W/2, sheet showing details of payment of bonus from the year 2005 to 20I3-l4, Banker cheque with respect to 
bonus, circulars with respect to minimum wages issued in different years from 2005-203, certificate issued by the 
Branch Manager on 4.05.20l] and note photocopy with respect to workers allotted and payment to the Bank for 
cleaning and certain vouchers with respect to payment, letters issued by the Branch Manager on |7.0.20I3 and 
03.09.203, to the Treasury Officer authorizing the workman to receive stamps issued by treasury, around 50 payment 
vouchers with respect to payment for cleaning from !.07.2009 to 20I, which are marked as Ex-W/] to Ex-W/25. 
The workman had filed Application seeking production of documents from management Bank. The Bank has filed 
copies of payment register for the period 03.04.200 to 06.07.203 with respect to payments regarding cleaning of the 
Branch to the claimant workman and other persons total 29 pages. 


Management has filed affidavit of its witness Mr. Sumit Gupta, he has been cross-examined by workman 
union. 


I have heard argument of Learned Counsel for workman Mr. Arun Patel and Mr. Praveen Yadav, Learned 
Counsel for management Bank. 


The reference itself is the issue for determination in the case in hand. 


The minimum bonus which a management is required to pay under section l0 of Bonus Act, is 8.33%. For, 
payment of bonus at higher rate, there has to be an agreement between the workman and management. No such 
agreement has been filed. Hence, action of management Bank in not paying bonus to the applicant workman @ 20% 
cannot be held to be unjustified. 


Hence, holding the demand of workman union for payment of bonus to the applicant workman Mr. 
Devendra Balram Gaud, @ 20%, unjustified, the reference stands answered accordingly.

According to the union, this action of management is in violation of Section 25-F and 25-G of the Act, 
hence is unjust, illegal and arbitrary. 


The union has requested that holding the disengagement of the workman Devendra Goud, by the 
management Bank, against law, he be held entitled to be reinstated with all back wages and benefits. 


According to the management Bank, the claimant was engaged on daily wages purely on temporary basis

Bank has denied the claim of the workman union that the workman worked continuously for a period of 240 days and

This is also the case of the management that the claimant workman was not appointed against any regular 
vacancy following recruitment process. He did not work for 240 days in any year, hence, his disengagement by the

In evidence, the workman union has filed affidavit of the workman Devendra Goud as his Examination-in- 
chief, he has been cross-examined by management Bank. 


He filed and proved Ex-W/I, Application before Labour Commissioner with respect to payment of bonus,

Issue No.|, 


Section 25-B of the Act, which defines ‘continuous service’, is being reproduced as follows:- 


“25B. Definition of continuous service.—For the purposes of this Chapter,— 


(7) a workman shall be said to be in continuous service for a period if he is, for that period, 
in uninterrupted service, including service which may be interrupted on account of 
sickness or authorised leave or an accident or a strike which is not illegal, or a lock-out 
or a cessation of work which is not due to any fault on the part of the workman; 


(2) where a workman is not in continuous service within the meaning of clause (2) for a 
period of one year or six months, he shall be deemed to be in continuous service under 
an employer— 


(a) for a period of one year, if the workman, during a period of twelve calendar 
months preceding the date with reference to which calculation is to be made, 
has actually worked under the employer for not less than— 


(i) one hundred and ninety days in the case of a workman employed below 
ground in a mine; and 


(ii) two hundred and forty days, in any other case; 


(b) for a period of six months, if the workman, during a period of six calendar 
months preceding the date with reference to which calculation is to be made, 
has actually worked under the employer for not less than— 


(i) ninety-five days, in the case of a workman employed below ground ina 
mine; and 
(ii) one hundred and twenty days, in any other case.” 


Pleadings of the parties on this issue have been detailed earlier. The workman has corroborated the allegation 
of the union on this issued. He has been cross-examined by management. He states that there was no advertisement 
released for the vacancy, no test conducted and also states that payments were made to him in different names. 


Learned Counsel for workman has submitted that he worked continuously with the bank for 240 days in 
every year and also in the year preceding the date of his termination i.e., 02.06.20I3 and this fact is established from 
the payment vouchers filed and proved by the workman, cash remittance register from November, 20!] to December, 
20] and from cash remittance register Naiabadi Branch from 03.0.20I] to 3.05.20i3 which have been filed by the 
Bank also in compliance of order of this Tribunal. 


Firstly, it is to be mentioned here that receiving payments by workman under different name is a crime, this 
is cheating by way of impersonation, hence, he cannot take advantage of his this statement.

On perusal of documents filed by him in support of his statement on oath, the certificate issued by the

which is bunch of 48 photocopy documents, vouchers relating to Manish Telecom, Manish Computer, Stationery 
and VIP Communication shows that payments were made to the firm of Manish with respect to supply of stationery, 
etc. May be the payment was received by the workman, but it does not show that the workman worked as an 
employee of management Bank. The two documents which are authorization letter dated 7.0i.20i3 and 03.09.20I3 
authorizing the workman to receive stamp from treasury only indicates that the workman was engaged for getting 
stamp from treasury on these dates. Another bunch of documents is Ex-22 which are 45 photocopy receipts related to

200. Thus, bunch of document also indicates that the claimant was paid for dates mentioned in these documents in 
different months in different years. This also does not corroborate fully the case of the workman, worked for 240 days 
in any year. 


The payment details filed by the management Bank under order of this Tribunal, as mentioned above, 
contain the name of the workman as well other persons also, to whom the payments were made by the Bank. The case 
of the workman union is that payments were made to him by Bank under fictitious names will not be counted in his 
favour. Thus, these documents also do not fully corroborate the case of the workman on the point of his continuous 
engagement of 240 days or more in a year or year preceding the date of termination. It is the case of the workman that 
he was paid in different bogus names, this fact also goes against him. On the other hand, management witness has 
stated that the workman never worked for 240 days in any year, he has mentioned number of days in which he worked 
with the Bank in a year and that too for cleaning of the branch. There are photocopy vouchers filed by the workman 
union showing that water payments were made to the workman with respect to procurement of water cans which he 
received on behalf of the firm. Hence, the case laws referred to by the learned counsel for workman union in their 
written arguments do not support them. It is already the case of the management that the workman was engaged

Hence, in light of this nature of evidence, the claim of the workman union that the applicant workman 
worked continuously for 240 days in any year or in a year preceding the date of disengagement is held not proved.

As per letter dated 5/06/202 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference 
has been made to this Tribunal under Section-l0 of Industrial Disputes Act, 947 (in short the ‘Act’) as per 
Notification No. 7-72077/20/2077077-7)) dt. 5/06/20i2. The dispute under reference relates to:- 


“Whether the demand of the Union, Dainik Vetan Bhogi Karamchari Sangathan, for appointment of Shri 
Santosh Kumar Sahu on regular basis w.e.f. 07/70/2007 with pay is legal and justified? To what relief the 
workman is entitled?” 


After registering the case on the basis of reference, notices were issued to the parties. They appeared and 
filed their respective statement of claim in defense. 


The case of the workman is mainly that he was first appointed as a daily wage Peon on 08.03.004 by the 
Branch Manager and worked 8 hours daily till 06.0.2007 without any notice or compensation, when he put up his 
claim for regularization of his service. According to the workman union, this action of management is in violation of 
Section 25-F and 25-G of the Act, hence unjust, illegal and arbitrary. 


It is also alleged that on the basis of his continuous service with the bank for three years, he is entitled to be 
regularized and denial of his this claim by the management bank is unjust, illegal and arbitrary. He has prayed that 
holding the action of management bank in terminating his service and no regularizing his service against law, he be 
held entitled to be reinstated and entitled to be regularized with all back wages and benefits. 


The case of the management bank is mainly that the workman was never appointed against any permanent 
vacancy of peon following any recruitment process. Hence, there was no occasion of his disengagement. According to 
the Bank, he was a daily wager, engaged by Bank as and when required on intermittent basis for which he was paid 
his daily wages. He never completed 240 days in any year; management has requested that the reference be answered 
against the workman.

In evidence, the workman has filed and proved order of Hon’ble High Court of M.P. dated 28.0.2004 in 
WP No. 48/2000, in which he was one of the petitioner’s, photocopy reply of Bank filed by them before the 
Regional Labour Commissioner during conciliation proceedings, photocopy letter of Bank dated 03.05.20i0 
regarding payment of bonus to the workman, photocopy cheque of bonus amount, which are marked as Ex-W/I to 
Ex-W/4. Workman union has further filed affidavit of the workman as his Examination-in-chief, he has been cross- 
examined by management. 


Management has filed and proved Ex-M/! and M/2 which are vouchers with respect to payment to the 
workman, management has further filed affidavit of its witnesses as his Examination-in-chief, he has been cross- 
examined by union. 


I have heard argument of Learned Counsel for workman Mr. Arun Patel and Mr. Praveen Yadav, Learned 
Counsel for the management bank. I have gone through the record as well. 


On perusal of record in light of rival arguments, following Issues came up for determination:- 


हे Whether the workman has successfully proved his continuous engagement with the management 
Bank as defined under section 25-B of the Act? 

2) Whether the action of management in disengaging the workman is legal? 

3) Subject to findings on issue No. | and 2, whether the workman is entitled to any relief? 

Issue No., 


Section 25-B of the Act, which defines ‘continuous service’, is being reproduced as follows:- 


“25B. Definition of continuous service.—For the purposes of this Chapter,— 


(7) a workman shall be said to be in continuous service for a period if he is, for that period, 
in uninterrupted service, including service which may be interrupted on account of 
sickness or authorised leave or an accident or a strike which is not illegal, or a lock-out 
or a cessation of work which is not due to any fault on the part of the workman; 


(2) where a workman is not in continuous service within the meaning of clause (7) for a 
period of one year or six months, he shall be deemed to be in continuous service under 
an employer— 


(a) for a period of one year, if the workman, during a period of twelve calendar 
months preceding the date with reference to which calculation is to be made, 
has actually worked under the employer for not less than— 


(i) one hundred and ninety days in the case of a workman employed below 
ground in a mine; and 


(ii) two hundred and forty days, in any other case; 


(b) for a period of six months, if the workman, during a period of six calendar 
months preceding the date with reference to which calculation is to be made, 
has actually worked under the employer for not less than— 


(i) ninety-five days, in the case of a workman employed below ground in a 
mine; and 
(ii) one hundred and twenty days, in any other case.” 


Pleadings of the parties on this issue have been detailed earlier. According to the workman he was appointed 
on the vacant post of Messenger in the branch in the year 99 by the then Branch Manager, he worked continuously 
for atleast 8 hours daily in the Bank. His services were earlier terminated by the Bank, he filed a writ petition No. 
48] /2000, he was reemployed by the Bank on 08.03.2004 in compliance of the order of Hon’ble High Court dated 
28.0.2004 and he worked continuously after his repayment till date of disengagement i.e., 06.l0.2007. 


He has further stated that he was paid bonus, also in his cross-examination, he has stated the he came to 
know about the vacancy from an advertisement released by the Bank, he had filled the form for appointment, he was 
interviewed by the Branch Manager, his name was not sponsored by employment ex-change, no interview letter was 
sent by the Bank. The Bank did not issue any appointment letter. 


He further states in his cross-examination that he did job of carrying documents from one counter to other, 
sent daak, carry cheques to clearing house and other works for which he was paid by the Bank. He admits that there 
was a canteen in the branch and he used to bring tea and snacks for the bank employees from the canteen.

There is on record, certified statement regarding payment to the workman which shows that during the 
period he was paid different amounts ranging from Rs. 30/- to Rs. 50/- by way of different vouchers for carrying 
cheques or other bank documents as well instruments to different places and visiting different places for bank works. 
There are also payments vouchers with respect to payment to him for filling water in the bank coolers etc. These 
vouchers show that he was paid the traveling expenses through these vouchers. When it is established that he had 
been reimbursed his travelling expenses during the period from 2004 to 2007 for visiting different places for banking 
work naturally, he would have been paid his wages also from the Bank, after all it cannot be assumed that he was 
doing this job only for reimbursement of his travelling expenses. These facts establish his engagement by the bank 
and also establish that he was engaged by the Bank in whatever capacity may be a daily wager. 


He has been paid bonus also, this fact also corroborates his statement with regard to his engagement with the 
Bank. On the other hand, there is on record affidavit of the management witness as his Examination-in-chief and his 
cross-examination in which he has stated that the workman was only assigned the work of Hamali as and when 
required basis and was paid remuneration for the work. Also that he worked only for 2 to 3 hours in a day. Infact, he 
was engaged as canteen boy by the local implementation committee for providing tea, water and snacks to the 
members, no appointment letter was issued by the Bank nor did he worked 240 days or more in any year. 


The witness also states that he did not follow the recruitment process. In his cross-examination, this witness 
states that it will be correct to say on the basis of salary payment reduced and available records that the workman was 
working in the same branch since 99 but he was working in which canteen, no record is available in this respect. He 
pleads ignorance that the Bank had taken an interview test of the workman for sub-staff in the year 997 and states 
that there is no record of employment of the workman management by local implementation committee, this witness 
further pleads ignorance regarding vacancy of peon in the said branch. 


On a comparative statement and evidence from both sides as mentioned above, it comes out that the case of 
management Bank that the workman was employed by the committee cannot be believed because there is no evidence 
except the statement of the management witness. There is no document in this respect, there is no evidence also in this 
respect. The management witness also admits that the workman used to do the Bank related works for which he was 
paid, his only point is that he did not work continuously for 240 days in a year. The documents in form of vouchers 
which show reimbursement of the workman on different dates with respect to the amount he incurred in travelling for 
the Bank work, that he worked regularly during the period from 2004 to 2007 these are the Bank certified documents. 


Thus, he is held to be a workman continuously for 240 days and more in every year including the year 
preceding the date of his disengagement as defined under section 25-B of the Act and the Bank is held to be his 
employer under the Act. 


Issue No. 4 is answered accordingly. 


Issue No. 2, 
Section 25-F & 25-G of the Act, is being reproduced as follows: 


25F. Conditions precedent to retrenchment of workmen. 


No workman employed in any industry who has been in continuous service for not less than one 
year under an employer shall be retrenched by that employer until- 


(a) the workman has been given one month's notice in writing indicating the reasons for 
retrenchment and the period of notice has expired, or the workman has been paid in lieu 
of such notice, wages for the period of the notice; 


(b) the workman has been paid, at the time of retrenchment, compensation which shall be 
equivalent to fifteen days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service or 
any part thereof in excess of six months; and 


(c) notice in the prescribed manner is served on the appropriate Government or such 
authority as may be specified by the appropriate Government by notification in the 
Official Gazette. 


25G Procedure _for_retrenchment.—Where any workman in an industrial establishment, who is a 
citizen of India, is to be retrenched and he belongs to a particular category of workmen in that 
establishment, in the absence of any agreement between the employer and the workman in this 
behalf, the employer shall ordinarily retrench the workman who was the last person to be 
employed in that category, unless for reasons to be recorded the employer retrenches any other 
workman. 


It is undisputed that no notice was issued to the workman before his disengagement nor was he paid any 
compensation. Hence his disengagement is held in violation of the act. 


Issue No. 2 stands answered accordingly.

Issue No. 3 


In light of aforesaid findings, the question arises as to relief to which the workman may be held entitled. 
Management, learned counsel has submitted that there is nothing on record to show that there was a regular vacancy 
at the time of his appointment, he was not sponsored by employment ex-change and he did not follow the recruitment 
process. Hence, his appointment is illegal. Thus he should not be reinstated on the finding forced in this argument 
from the side of the Bank. 


Learned counsel for the workman has stated that he has been working with the Bank as a daily wager since 
99. He was once disengaged in the year 2000 and was reinstated under order of Hon’ble High Court in 2004, again 
disengaged arbitrarily in 2007, he requires to be reinstated with backwages and benefits. 


There is force in the argument of management for the appointment of the workman was not through 
recruitment process, hence, not a regular appointment, a lump sum compensation quantified Rs. lLac/- in lieu of all 
his claims will meet the ends of justice which the workman is held entitled to be paid by the Bank within 30 days 
from the date of publication of the award, failing which interest @ 6% p.a. from the date of award till payment. 


In light of above discussion and findings, the reference is answered as follows.-

“Holding the action of the management in disengaging the workman Santosh Kumar Sahu from

within 30 days from the date of publication award, failing which interest @ 6% p.a. from the date of award till 
payment, in lieu of all his claims.” 


No order as to cost.
